case.caption: State of Utah v. Tyler James Robinson
case.court: Fourth Judicial District Court, Provo, Utah County

principle: This tracker holds officials accountable to the documentary record. It logs findings against the state, evidentiary gaps, and challenges raised by counsel — each labeled for what it actually is. A sanctioned violation and a contested assertion are recorded differently on purpose: collapsing them would make the tracker unusable for its own purpose. Every entry names the document that would confirm or refute it.

sanctioned.label: Court-sanctioned violations
sanctioned.desc: A judge made a formal finding that a rule or order was violated. The strongest category — these are not allegations.

evidence_gap.label: Documented evidence gaps
evidence_gap.desc: Holes in the evidentiary record that are established fact, not argument.

contested.label: Contested on the record
contested.desc: Raised by counsel in open court. Being raised is not the same as being sustained — that distinction is preserved here deliberately.

transparency.label: Disclosure & transparency
transparency.desc: Disputes over what the public, press, and parties could see.

unresolved.label: Unresolved / actionable
unresolved.desc: Open questions with a specific document that would settle them.

entries.title: Prosecutor Christopher Ballard held in civil contempt over a 'media tour'
entries.what_happened: UPDATED with confirmed detail: Robinson's own defense filed the motion that triggered this. It alleged prosecutor Christopher Ballard — who is both a prosecutor on the case and the Utah County Attorney's Office spokesman — went on a willful 'media tour,' publicly stating there was 'ample evidence' to prove Robinson's guilt before trial, in violation of the court's pretrial publicity restrictions. Judge Tony Graf Jr. found Ballard in civil contempt and ordered Robinson's defense reimbursed for the costs of pursuing the motion. The judge declined the defense's separate request to bar prosecutors from seeking the death penalty.
entries.status: Court found a violation; defense costs reimbursed; death penalty remains on the table
entries.verification_note: This is a formal judicial finding of a violation, not an allegation or a defense assertion left unresolved — the court ruled and imposed a remedy. Note it was Robinson's own defense that brought the motion, which matters for evaluating the parallel contempt/withholding motion logged separately below (C15).
entries.what_would_resolve: Already resolved by the court's ruling. The remaining open question is the exact language of Ballard's public statements, available in the contempt order itself on the docket.

entries.title: Evidence displayed in violation of the court's own orders
entries.what_happened: A handwritten note attributed to the defendant was visible on the public feed for roughly three seconds. Judge Graf ruled the publication violated the court's orders and responded by barring media from broadcasting any evidence shown in court. Final video evidence was consequently withheld from the public livestream.
entries.status: Court found its orders violated; remedial restriction imposed
entries.what_would_resolve: The order itself, from the docket, for its exact scope and duration.

entries.title: Body camera gap during the roof examination
entries.what_happened: Body camera footage from investigator Christopher Bagley contained gaps. His battery died while he was examining the Losee Center roof — the location from which the shot was reportedly fired. The roof examination is therefore incompletely documented.
entries.status: Documented gap; surfaced by the defense on the record
entries.what_would_resolve: Bagley's testimony transcript and any written report covering the roof examination; the department's BWC policy on battery management and documentation of gaps.
entries.note: Bagley also appears in the Trends claim dataset as a matched control.

entries.title: Pistol holster recovered but never fingerprinted
entries.what_happened: Defense counsel Kathryn Nester established that a pistol holster was discovered and never processed for fingerprints. She used this, together with a legally carried concealed weapon found on campus, to argue investigators had not adequately excluded other shooters.
entries.status: Documented investigative omission; raised on the record
entries.what_would_resolve: Evidence log and lab submission records for the holster; the investigative decision memo, if one exists, explaining why it was not processed.

entries.title: Limits of forensic certainty — ATF testimony
entries.what_happened: The defense called two ATF witnesses on DNA reliability. ATF forensic biologist Caitlin Oliver (described as DNA Section Chief in some reporting) testified: "With forensic evidence, it's impossible to state with 100% certainty anything." The prosecution's figure was that the DNA was 30 quintillion times more likely to be Robinson's than an unrelated individual's.
entries.status: Contested — a statement about the general limits of forensic science, not a defect found in this analysis
entries.what_would_resolve: The full lab reports and the analysts' bench notes, which would show the actual protocol, controls, and any deviations.
entries.note: Worth reading precisely: Oliver stated a truism about forensic science generally. That is different from testimony that this particular analysis was flawed. The tracker records the distinction rather than flattening it.

entries.title: Broad defense objections to evidence admission
entries.what_happened: The defense spent much of the five-day hearing contesting admission of evidence on hearsay, public-access, and fair-trial grounds.
entries.what_would_resolve: The hearing transcripts and the court's rulings on each objection.

entries.title: Enhanced surveillance compilation — courtroom only
entries.what_happened: Judge Graf permitted an enhanced security-footage compilation for courtroom viewing while withholding it from media access. Three assassination videos were shown on monitors only, not to the gallery.
entries.status: Disclosed and litigated in open court
entries.what_would_resolve: The enhancement methodology and who performed it — obtainable through the discovery record or expert disclosures.
entries.note: KEY FINDING for the image-processing question. Enhancement was used, and it was disclosed to the court and to defense counsel and ruled on in open proceedings. The restriction governed public broadcast, not defense access. Nothing in the record indicates concealed alteration.

entries.title: Motions regarding prosecutor conflicts
entries.what_happened: Pretrial motion practice concerning asserted conflicts of interest on the prosecution team.
entries.verification_note: Nature of the asserted conflicts and their disposition are not established here.
entries.what_would_resolve: The conflict motions and the court's ruling, from the docket.

entries.title: Sealing disputes and subsequent unsealing
entries.what_happened: The first in-person hearing addressed press access to filings. The court later denied a request to seal filings, and subsequently unsealed documents in the case.
entries.what_would_resolve: The sealing and unsealing orders from the docket.

entries.title: Conflicting reports on the post-hearing schedule
entries.what_happened: Herald Extra reported the court would reconvene September 1, 2026 for final arguments and a ruling. Deseret News reported Judge Graf granted the defense's request to proceed on written briefs instead of oral argument, with decisions due late July to mid-August 2026. The two accounts disagree.
entries.what_would_resolve: The scheduling order in case 251403576. As of 2026-08-12 the Deseret window has elapsed, so a ruling may already be filed.

entries.title: Fatal projectile comparison was inconclusive — named examiner
entries.what_happened: An ATF firearms examiner identified in testimony as Samantha Karner testified that comparison of the recovered bullet fragment with the suspected murder rifle was INCONCLUSIVE, and explicitly rejected attempts to characterize the result as anything stronger. This corrects in both directions: 'the bullet didn't match the rifle' is wrong, and so is 'ballistics proved this rifle fired the fatal shot.'
entries.verification_note: In a textbook sniper prosecution the recovered rifle → fatal bullet linkage would be among the cleanest evidence. Here it is not. This raises the evidentiary importance of the rifle's PROVENANCE — where it was found, by whom, and after what prior searches — far above what it would be with a pristine individualizing match.
entries.what_would_resolve: The full examiner's report and bench notes, the comparison microscopy documentation, and any second-examiner verification. Whether the inconclusive result reflects fragment condition, barrel wear, or a genuine exclusion question is not publicly established.

entries.title: K9 and line-search sequence preceding the rifle's discovery
entries.what_happened: The FBI announced on September 11, 2025 that the rifle — an older .30-06 Mauser wrapped in a towel — had been recovered in a wooded area along the escape route. At the July 2026 hearing, former Utah SBI agent David Hull testified surveillance showed Robinson entering that wooded area twice. A more specific allegation now circulating holds that local officers performed a line search without finding it, K9s then searched without finding it, and only after federal agents directed another search of the same area did junior local officers find it.
entries.status: UNVERIFIED — the allegation's own source labels it uncorroborated
entries.verification_note: The claimed sequence was found reproduced on an investigative website that ITSELF labels it uncorroborated, noting its underlying list provides no officer name, report number, timestamp, K9 record or primary source. Ordinary explanations are available: a patrol/tracking dog searching for a fleeing human performs a fundamentally different task from a firearms-detection dog trained to alert on gunpowder odor; dense vegetation, wind, handler direction, search boundaries and towel-wrapping all matter; humans routinely miss objects on first search; and 'the FBI searched the area' is not the same claim as 'the area had previously been searched' when multiple agencies were operating there. This is listed because it is unusually RESOLVABLE, not because it is established.
entries.what_would_resolve: K9 handler's report and the dog's certification/specialty; GPS or search-track records; bodycam from both the initial search and the discovery; search-team and scene perimeter logs; exact rifle coordinates; photographs before anything was touched; first-recovery timestamp; and evidence packaging and chain-of-custody documentation. If bodycam or GPS proves someone walked directly past the eventual location with an appropriate detection K9 and the rifle later appeared there, that would become one of the strongest anomalies in the case.

entries.title: UVU security posture at an open-air event for a threatened figure
entries.what_happened: Approximately 3,000 people attended an open-air appearance by a nationally prominent and routinely threatened political figure. AP found UVU deployed six officers, conducted no bag or metal-detector screening, did not use a drone to monitor surrounding rooftops, and did not coordinate with outside law enforcement. The courtyard was ringed by elevated buildings offering obvious firing positions. Kirk's security chief Brian Harpole later publicly displayed what he said were communications showing his team had specifically discussed rooftop security with UVU police beforehand, alleging assurances were given that the roofs would be addressed.
entries.status: Documented failure; the pre-event rooftop assurance remains unadjudicated
entries.verification_note: CONTROL CASE: the July 13, 2024 Butler rally shooting establishes that even the Secret Service ecosystem, after extensive advance planning, left a known high-risk elevated position unsecured — as the bipartisan House investigation and DHS inspector-general work both found. So UVU's rooftop failure is extraordinary evidence of NEGLIGENCE. It is not, by itself, evidence of deliberate facilitation. Countervailing: reporting indicates the student organization's event paperwork badly understated the event's risk profile, and UVU policies gave inadequate guidance for evaluating high-risk speakers.
entries.what_would_resolve: UVU's independent security review — announced shortly after the killing — has still not produced a public accounting. The specific records needed are the advance-planning documents, the TPUSA–UVU communications Harpole references, the event risk assessment, and the assignment roster for the six officers.

entries.title: Defense moved to strike the death-penalty aggravating factor
entries.what_happened: Robinson's attorneys asked the judge to strike the only aggravating factor that makes him death-penalty eligible, arguing prosecutors failed to present enough evidence at the preliminary hearing that Robinson 'knowingly created a great risk of death to another other than Charlie Kirk' — the specific statutory basis charged. Separately, the defense filed a motion addressing preservation of ballistics evidence and expert observation of any further testing, tied directly to the ATF's inability to identify the recovered bullet to the rifle.
entries.status: Pending — folded into the September 1, 2026 probable-cause briefing
entries.verification_note: A live, contested legal argument rather than a settled fact either way. Directly connects to the inconclusive-ballistics finding already logged (Assessment tab anomaly A1; Conduct C11) — the defense is using that same evidentiary gap as the basis for a specific, formal motion, not just public commentary.
entries.what_would_resolve: The written ruling on the aggravating-factor motion, expected as part of the September 1, 2026 probable-cause decision.

entries.title: Defense alleges withheld evidence — separate from the Ballard contempt motion
entries.what_happened: Distinct from the Ballard 'media tour' contempt finding (C01): Robinson's defense separately asked the court to order Utah County Attorney Jeff Gray's office to turn over evidence the defense claims is being withheld. This is a discovery dispute, not a publicity violation — a direct, sourced allegation from the defense itself about the completeness of the state's disclosures, which is a materially stronger category of claim than third-party speculation about hidden evidence circulating online.
entries.status: Pending — no public ruling identified as of this entry
entries.verification_note: An allegation from a party with direct discovery access and a legal obligation to the court when making it — not proof the state is actually withholding anything. Worth tracking to a resolution specifically because it is the highest-credibility version of a 'hidden evidence' claim currently on the record, in contrast to the many unsourced online versions.
entries.what_would_resolve: The court's ruling on the discovery motion, and — if granted — what was actually produced as a result.

entries.title: Robinson's own defense opposes public release of the UVU security plan
entries.actor: Defense + Utah Valley University + Government Records Office
entries.what_happened: FOX13 requested UVU's security plan for the TPUSA event under Utah's public-records law. UVU denied the request citing exemptions for security measures, law-enforcement activity, and the right to a fair trial; Utah's Government Records Office ruled against release. When FOX13 appealed, ROBINSON'S OWN DEFENSE TEAM intervened in a 12-page letter supporting UVU's denial — arguing the security plan is a protected record whose release could taint Robinson's trial and interfere with multiple ongoing investigations.
entries.status: Records remain sealed; defense position is on the public docket
entries.verification_note: GENUINE TENSION WORTH TRACKING: much of the public discourse around this case treats UVU's security failure as something the defendant's side would want fully exposed, since it supports an alternative-explanation or reduced-culpability narrative. Instead, the one party positioned to benefit most from that record's disclosure is actively working to keep it sealed. The likeliest explanation is conventional and unremarkable — fair-trial and pretrial-publicity protection is standard defense practice, and a public security failure narrative can be built at trial without a public document dump beforehand. But it is a concrete, sourced data point that cuts against the simplest version of 'the defense wants everything exposed,' and it belongs in the record rather than being smoothed over.
entries.what_would_resolve: Trial itself, where the security-planning record would need to be introduced if the defense intends to use it — or a change in the sealing order beforehand.

entries.title: UVU document production to media came back heavily redacted
entries.what_happened: The Daily Caller obtained a batch of UVU records related to the shooting through a public-records request; the production came back with extensive redactions. Separately, FOX13's own long-running document request from UVU has been repeatedly denied and is the subject of the ongoing appeal referenced in C16.
entries.status: Redacted records now public; underlying unredacted material remains withheld
entries.verification_note: Standard practice for records touching an active capital case and an ongoing security review can produce exactly this pattern without implying concealment beyond what the law already permits — but it is a concrete, dated instance of the general transparency gap this app has tracked throughout (see C13's still-missing UVU security review), not a new theory.
entries.what_would_resolve: UVU's still-outstanding independent security review, and resolution of the FOX13 appeal.

entries.title: Judicial Watch lawsuit for site cleanup and paving records
entries.actor: Judicial Watch (third-party litigant) v. Utah Valley University
entries.what_happened: Judicial Watch filed a formal lawsuit — not merely a GRAMA request — seeking records related to a paving operation at the shooting site, citing 'intense public interest in the political assassination of Charlie Kirk.' This corroborates the site-cleanup/paving records production already referenced by CharlieFiles.com's site index, but confirms it reached the level of actual litigation rather than a pending records request.
entries.verification_note: The first identified civil litigant in this case unconnected to any of the direct parties (prosecution, defense, TPUSA, or named individuals) — a useful category distinct from everything else logged here because it's motivated by public-records transparency law specifically, not by a personal or institutional stake in the outcome.
entries.what_would_resolve: The records themselves, once produced through the litigation.

access_note: Utah publishes no bulk docket data. Case-specific filings require Utah Court Xchange ($0.35 per search, $1.00 per document) or a free terminal at the Fourth District Courthouse (125 N 100 W, Provo) or the Utah State Law Library. The weekly district CSV reports retain only the two most recent weeks and carry no charges or docket entries, so September 2025 is not retrievable there.
